sentences: A pair-oared racing boat carrying two brothers swings around a stake planted in the middle of the river.
The long, slim shell cuts across the picture, with the wide river and its green banks opening out behind.
Everything is bathed in clear, even daylight.
John and Barney Biglin were celebrated professional oarsmen from New York.
The painting shows the halfway turn of a famous five-mile race on Philadelphia's Schuylkill River in May 1872.
It was a match that the newspapers followed closely.
Look at the stake beside the boat.
Topped with a blue flag, it marks the halfway point of the course.
The shell has all but completed its pivot and is about to head back the way it came.
The pole stands perfectly straight while the boat swings around it.
Now look at the brothers' heads.
Both wear blue kerchiefs, and the trim of their shirts, the stake flag and the water around them are all cool blues, a colour that ties the picture together.
Set against the warm brown of the boat, the blue makes the pair stand out.
Notice the matched angle of the two oars.
One brother pulls hard while the other balances the boat through the turn.
Both heads are slightly bowed, their faces full of quiet concentration.
This is teamwork made visible.
The rival crew, wearing red kerchiefs, trails behind on the right.
They were a pair from Pittsburgh.
The Biglins won that race by a full minute and were hailed as champions.
Spectators line the far bank.
Rowing was one of America's most popular spectator sports in the 1870s, and this race is said to have drawn a large crowd to the river.
Look closely and you can pick out tiny figures all along the shore.
Eakins himself rowed on the Schuylkill long before he trained in Paris.
He painted oarsmen again and again, and the Biglin brothers were among his favourite subjects.
For him this was a picture of teamwork as much as of a race.
He planned each boat and figure with precise perspective drawings before painting, so the distances in the picture can actually be measured.
Even the reflections on the water are carefully placed.
This care for exact measurement runs through all of his work.
At lower left he signed his name with the year 73.
Still unsold when he died in 1916, the picture passed to his widow, who sold it to the Cleveland Museum of Art in 1927.
It has belonged to the museum ever since.
Step back once more.
Eakins chose not the moment of victory, but the turn where the race is decided.
Feel that brief instant when two rowers breathe and pull as one.
